Morse Keyboard

The same program with two receive-side changes, highlighted below, so ordinary Morse spacing decodes.

Back to the program Original listing Download .txt (18 KB)

What this program does

A Morse code keyboard for the Radio Shack Color Computer. In transmit mode you type text and it keys a transmitter and sounds a tone. In receive mode it listens to a tone decoder wired to the cassette input and prints what it hears. It runs on the screen's 32 by 16 text display, so there is no graphics and no sprites.

Almost all of the program is timing loops. The 6809 has no timers, so every duration is made by counting passes of a loop whose cycle cost is known, at the Color Computer's 0.895 MHz clock. Every long loop calls Color BASIC's keyboard poll (POLCAT, through the vector at $A000) on each pass, so keys keep working while it sends or listens. That poll is also the main part of each pass's cost, which is why speeds come out right only with the real routine in place.

In the browser, POLCAT is replaced by a small stand-in that burns the same number of cycles. Measured passes: the tone loop in SOUND about 766 cycles, the polling loops in the receiver about 690 to 700, the debounce loops 25, and the word-gap loop 30.

The hardware it uses

The program touches only a few hardware addresses. $FF20 is the sound DAC when written, and bit 0 reads the cassette input when read. Bit 3 of $FF21 switches the cassette motor relay, which this program uses as the transmitter key. $FF23 bit 3 enables sound, $FF01 bit 3 selects the DAC as the sound source, and $FF22 picks the text colors.

Bit 0 of $FF20 is the cassette input's comparator, a zero-crossing detector. With the radio's earphone audio plugged in, it is the polarity of the waveform: while a tone is present it flips at the tone's frequency, and with no tone it sits still at IR, which is 255, so a read of 1. The receiver times those flips, and counts passes of its loops to measure how long a tone lasts.

It does not measure the pitch. It only needs to know whether a tone is there. A flip is not a tone; a tone is a stream of flips with no gap of 25 readings in a row at the idle level (see R2).

AddressWhat the program keeps or does there
$FF20Written: 6-bit sound DAC (a square wave of $FC and $04 makes the tone). Read: bit 0 is the cassette input, the received key line.
$FF21Bit 3 is the cassette motor relay. Set while sending a tone, so it keys the transmitter.
$FF22 / $FF23$FF22 is set to 8, the VDG color set bit, giving orange text. $FF23 bit 3 enables sound.
$FF01Bit 3 selects the sound source. Cleared for the tone, set again afterward.
$A000Vector to Color BASIC POLCAT, the keyboard poll. Returns a key in A, or zero.
$0400-$05FFThe 32 x 16 text screen. Row 0 is the header. Rows 1 to 7 show received text, rows 8 to 14 show text you send, row 15 is the help line.
$03E3Top of the stack (set at START).
$3462-$3D83This program: variables first ($3465-$348C), then code, then the Morse table at $3D43. Entry is BEGIN at $3462.
$3D83-$3FFEThe send buffer (STACK). BSTK is the next character to send, ESTK is where the next typed one goes.

Trying it

Open the program page and press S, type a speed such as 15 or 20, then press Enter. Up arrow is transmit mode, down arrow is receive. Station B on the page is a second copy of the program that sends to your receiver, and the Recording panel plays an mp3 or other audio file into it.

As printed, the receiver decodes this program's own sending rhythm (a gap inside a letter of about 0.43 dit) but not ordinary Morse, where that gap is one dit. Tried on a real on-air recording (an Italian ragchew on 7036 kHz, about 36 WPM, played at 16 to 36 WPM), the printed program gives strings of E and T. The patched listing reads the same recording as text, for example PER I I Z 8 VKW RST 5NN, with the letters running together a little (FATT O, L A LUIGI) where a long dah or a pause falls near a threshold.

The pitch of a recording does not matter in the page's tone decoder mode, which finds the tone and gives the program a clean on/off line. With the raw zero-crossing input, the program only decodes at certain pitches, because it samples the line once per polling pass. The usable pitches fall around 1200 to 1400 Hz.

The 16 highlighted lines are the changes: how the letter-gap threshold TSP is worked out (lines 06300 to 06400), and the word-gap threshold TEMP with a keyboard poll added to R18 (lines 07420 to 07466). Everything else is as printed.

Whenever the polarity reads idle, it checks for 25 idle readings in a row (TIME) in a tight loop, R50, each reading about 25 cycles, so a window of about 0.7 ms. If a tone reading shows up inside the window the polarity is still flipping, so the tone continues and the count carries on. Only a still polarity for the whole window ends the tone. That is how short flips, the half-cycles of the tone and brief noise, are ignored, and how the end of a tone is noticed. For this to work a tone's half-cycle must be shorter than the window, so the pitch must be above about 700 Hz.Every time that window fails, the readings it used are added to the count, as well as the one pass of the slower loop. The length measured therefore is not a clean count of passes; it is inflated by an amount that depends on how the tone's flips line up with the loop's samples (about three times at 1200 Hz in the emulator). When the alignment is steady through a tone, the inflation is steady and dit and dah stay in proportion. At some pitches the alignment slides slowly against the loop and the lengths vary a lot from tone to tone. That is the preferred pitch effect: in the emulator a clean 1200, 1400 and 1800 Hz tone works, and 1300 Hz does not.05490 R2      LEAX 1,X05500         PSHS X05510         LBSR UPSTK05520         LDA RFLG05530         BEQ R3405540         LBRA RCVR05550 R34     LDA JXMT05560         BEQ R3505570         LBRA XMIT05580 R35     LDA RSTR05590         BEQ R8205600         LBRA START05610 R82     PULS X05620 R28     LDA $FF2005630         ORA #$FE05640         CMPX TMID05650         BRN R205660         CMPA IR05670         BNE R205680         LDB TIME+105690 R50     LDA $FF2005700         ORA #$FE05710         LEAX 1,X05720         CMPA IR05730         BEQ R5105740         BRA R205750 R51     DECB05760         BNE R50End of a toneThe 25 readings used for the check were counted as passes, so they are subtracted. X is now the tone's length.05770         LEAX -25,XLearning dit and dahThe first tone becomes T1. Then the loop goes back and measures a second, T2. If the two are equal, or less than half apart, it ignores the second and waits for another tone. Once they differ enough, it sorts them (short is a dit, long is a dah) and works out the thresholds below. It learns only once; a restart is needed to learn again.Because T1 and T2 are the first two tones heard, the first character of a message is used up by learning. Send a short character such as V first.05780         LDA FLAG05790         BNE R305800         STX T105810         INC FLAG05820         LDX #005830         LBRA R105840 R3      STX T205850         CMPX T105860         BNE R405870         LDX #005880         LBRA R105890 R4      BLT R505900         TFR X,D05910         SUBD T105920         TFR D,X05930         LDD T105940         LSRA05950         RORB05960         STD TEMP05970         CMPX TEMP05980         BGE R705990         LDX #006000         LBRA R106010 R5      LDX T106020         TFR X,D06030         SUBD T206040         TFR D,X06050         LDD T206060         LSRA06070         RORB06080         STD TEMP06090         CMPX TEMP06100         BGE R906110         LDX #006120         LBRA R106130 R9      LDX T106140         LDY T206150         STX T206160         STY T1R7: the thresholdsTMID is halfway between a dit and a dah. TF is half a dit, below which a tone is noise. T3 is the longest tone allowed (a dah plus TMID). Anything longer sends the receiver back to the start.06170 R7      LDD T206180         SUBD T106190         LSRA06200         RORB06210         ADDD T106220         STD TMID06230         LDD T106240         LSRA06250         RORB06260         STD TF06270         LDD T206280         ADDD TMID06290         STD T3TSP: when a letter ends (patched)TSP is now 2.25 times TMID plus 25. With the three-per-pass counting in R14, that ends a letter after 0.75 times TMID passes of silence, which is about 1.5 dits for a 1:3 dit/dah ratio. It sits between the gap inside a letter (0.43 dit for this program, 1 dit for ordinary Morse) and the gap between letters (2.2 dits, or 3).06300         LDD TMID06310         LSRA06320         RORB06330         LSRA06340         RORB06350         STD TEMP06360         LDD TMID06370         ADDD TMID06380         ADDD TEMP06390         ADDD #2506400         STD TSPDecodingFrom here each element is measured and added to RC. RC starts as 1; a dit shifts it left, a dah shifts it left and adds one. That leaves the same format TABLE uses: a leading 1 followed by the elements.06450         CLR RC06460         INC RC06470         LDA #806480         STA MCTR11: wait for the next toneWaits while the line is idle. At the first sign of a tone it moves on to measure it.06490 R11     LDA $FF2006500         ORA #$FE06510         PSHS A06520         LBSR UPSTK06530         LDA RFLG06540         BEQ R4706550         LBRA RCVR06560 R47     LDA JXMT06570         BEQ R4806580         LBRA XMIT06590 R48     LDA RSTR06600         BEQ R8406610         LBRA START06620 R84     PULS A06630         CMPA IR06640         BEQ R11The corner lightsThe two cells at the top left of the screen, $0400 and $0401, are set to $9F (yellow) and $AF (blue) in opposite order at the start of each tone here, and swapped back when it ends (R45). So from this point they flash as tones come and go. Nothing flashes in the corner while the receiver is still learning, so the first flash means the dit and dah lengths are known and it is decoding. The cell beside them, $0405, flips color after each finished letter, and $0403 flips each time receiving restarts with nothing heard.
